11 Resources/departments/ultimate-ai-boo.text:
---
name: ultimate-ai-book-builder
description: >
  Extend and rebuild "The Ultimate AI Book" — a large Word (.docx) book generated by a
  modular python-docx build. Use when adding a new section, adding a language/tool sub-section
  to the Coding Series (Section 36), enriching text, building matplotlib figure mockups, or
  rebuilding and verifying the book. Trigger on: "add a section to the AI book", "new coding
  series language", "add figures/screenshots", "rebuild the book".
metadata:
  type: project
---

# Ultimate AI Book — build & extend

## 0. Where things live
- **Deliverable:** `Content Creation/Content Playbook/The Ultimate AI Book.docx`
- **Source (this folder):** `Content Creation/Content Playbook/Ultimate AI Book - Build Source/`
  - `pp2_build.py` — the master build; `exec()`s every section module in order, then `doc.save(...)`.
  - `cp_base.py` — base helpers (`doc`, `H1/H2/H3`, `P`, `LEAD`, `INS`, `PB`, colours NAVY/BLUE/GREEN/GREY/SUBT/BLACK, `_setfont`).
  - `expert_arch.py` — defines `TABLE`, `HEADERBOX`; `pp2_build.py` also hoists `B`, `NUM`, `MNUM`, `BOXA`, `FIGIMG`, `SECTIONDIV`, `SUBGROUP`, `add_hyperlink`.
  - `<section>.py` — one module per section/sub-section (content only).
  - `render_*.py` — matplotlib figure renderers → write PNGs into `figs/<tool>/`.
  - `figs/` — all figure PNGs (already embedded in the built docx).
- **Working copy for editing/rebuilding:** copy this whole folder into the session scratch/outputs dir, edit there, rebuild, then copy the new `.docx` (and any changed source) back here. The scratch dir is wiped between sessions — this folder is the persistent truth.

## 1. House-style helpers (call these; do not restyle by hand)
`SECTIONDIV("Section N","Title","blurb")` (once per top-level section) · `SUBGROUP("Label","desc")` (a navigable sub-section within a section) · `H1/H2/H3("t")` · `LEAD("t")` · `P("t", after=6)` · `INS("t")` (italic call-out) · `B("Bold lead || rest")` (bold-lead bullet; `||` splits) · `NUM("t")` / `MNUM([...])` (numbered) · `TABLE([headers],[[row],...],[widths],bold_cols=(0,))` · `HEADERBOX(["line",...])` (monospace box for code/commands) · `FIGIMG(path,"caption")` (embeds a PNG at 6.3in + caption) · `PB()` (page break).
Text is in **double-quoted** Python strings; for lines containing double quotes use **single-quoted** Python strings. British English. Never place `P/B/INS` inside a `TABLE`/`HEADERBOX`/`MNUM` list — those take strings only.

## 2. Add a NEW top-level section
1. Write `mysection.py` starting with `SECTIONDIV("Section N","...","...")` then content; end with `PB()`.
2. In `pp2_build.py`: insert `exec(open('.../mysection.py').read(), globals())` **before** the `agentic_syllabus.py` exec (the syllabus is the last, capstone section).
3. Renumber the syllabus: bump its `SECTIONDIV("Section N",...)` up by one.
4. Update the Contents `SECTIONS=[...]` list in `pp2_build.py` (add the new entry, bump the syllabus entry).
5. Rebuild + verify (Section 4/5 below).

## 3. Add a sub-section to the Coding Series (Section 36)
Sub-sections live in separate `webdev_<lang>.py` modules that start with `SUBGROUP("Lang — ...","desc")` and define `WEBFIG="/.../figs/webdev"` at the top. They are spliced into `webdev_section.py` via `exec(open('.../webdev_<lang>.py').read(), globals())` placed **before the final `PB()`**. No renumbering needed (it is one section). Then rebuild.

## 4. Figure renderers (matplotlib, offline)
Copy the closest existing `render_*.py` and adapt. Conventions:
- `matplotlib.use("Agg")`; `fig=plt.figure(figsize=(10,6.25),dpi=170)`; `ax=fig.add_axes([0,0,1,1])`; `ax.set_xlim(0,100); ax.set_ylim(0,62.5); ax.axis("off")`.
- Save with `fig.savefig(out, facecolor=BG)` — **do NOT** use `bbox_inches="tight"` (breaks any `fig.add_axes` sub-charts / alignment).
- **Editor+result panels:** left dark editor `#1e2530` + right white "browser" or dark "terminal/console" panel. Reuse: `render_webdev.py` (code+browser), `render_webdev_py.py`/`_js.py` (code+console), `render_webdev_sql.py` (result grid), `render_webdev_kotlin.py`/`_swift.py` (phone mockups), `render_api.py`/`render_docker.py`/`render_devops.py` (diagrams + arrows + `mono()`).
- Syntax colours: keywords `#4aa8ff`, types `#4ec9b0`, builtins/decorators `#dcdcaa`, strings `#e0a45e`, numbers `#b5cea8`, comments `#6a8a99`, normal text `#d5dde5`.
- Monospace advance in the shared `mono()` helper: `x += len(text)*fs*0.142`.
- **GOTCHAS (learned the hard way):**
  - matplotlib draws **text above filled shapes** regardless of call order → never leave text where an overlay panel/popup will cover it; keep that area clear or the behind-text bleeds through.
  - **No emoji / unusual glyphs** — DejaVu renders them as boxes. Draw icons, phone frames, buttons, logos as shapes. Safe glyphs: letters, digits, `○ ● ■ ▶ ✓ ★ ↑ ↓ → + − / : . , < > ( ) { } [ ]`. After rendering, grep stderr for `missing from font` and replace any flagged glyph.
  - Keep code panels to ~10-14 short lines so nothing overflows the panel width.
- Wire the produced PNGs with `FIGIMG(FIG+"/name.png","caption")` in the section module.

## 5. Rebuild + verify (IMPORTANT: build exceeds the 45s shell limit)
Run the build **detached** so it survives the shell timeout, then poll:
```
cd <scratch outputs dir>
rm -f /tmp/build.log /tmp/build.done
setsid bash -c 'python3 pp2_build.py > /tmp/build.log 2>&1; touch /tmp/build.done' </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 &
disown; sleep 44; cat /tmp/build.log | tail -3; ls /tmp/build.done && echo DONE
```
Then VERIFY (a shell-killed build can corrupt the .docx):
```
python3 - <<'PY'
import zipfile,re
p="/.../The Ultimate AI Book.docx"
z=zipfile.ZipFile(p); assert z.testzip() is None            # zip valid (not truncated)
xml=z.read("word/document.xml").decode("utf-8","ignore")
bms=set(re.findall(r'w:name="([^"]+)"',xml)); anch=set(re.findall(r'w:anchor="([^"]+)"',xml))
print("anchors w/o bookmark:", sorted(anch-bms))                     # must be []
print("media:", sum(1 for n in z.namelist() if n.startswith('word/media/')))
PY
```
- **Navigation integrity:** every internal link (`w:anchor`) must resolve to a bookmark (`w:name`); `section_1..N` bookmarks must all exist. `SECTIONDIV` bookmarks `section_<num>` + `toc_top` back-buttons; the Contents links to `section_{num}`.
- Note: table-cell text is NOT in `Document(path).paragraphs` — search `word/document.xml` (unescape HTML entities) to verify content inside tables.
- After a good build, copy the new `.docx` back to the Playbook folder and any changed `.py`/PNG back into this Build Source folder.

## 6. Delivering
Share the `.docx` with `mcp__cowork__present_files`. Remind the user: it is Dropbox-synced (double-click to download if it shows online-only) and Word internal links need Ctrl+Click.

11 Resources/skills/full-site-audit/SKIL.text:
---
name: "full-site-audit"
description: "Exhaustively audit a COMPLETE website — every inner page per the sitemap, and every section/component on each page — and prove the coverage. Use whenever Ahmed wants to confirm an order/change was executed across ALL pages without misses, or wants a full-site QA. Triggers on: audit the whole website / every page, sitemap audit, \"did you review every section on every page\", \"make sure the change applied to all pages\", coverage matrix, \"no page or section missed\", full-site QA, review all inner pages. Works on local HTML builds (single-file view-router apps and multi-page sites). Enumerate-then-audit with a completion gate that FAILS if any page or section is unreviewed; delivers a Dashboard-001-style HTML scorecard (pages × sections, PASS/FAIL) plus a Markdown sign-off ledger and a Ship / Fix-first verdict."
---

# Full-Site Audit — Sitemap-Driven, Coverage-Guaranteed

Audit an **entire website** — every inner page in the sitemap, and **every section and component on each page** — and *prove* nothing was skipped. Built to answer one question with evidence: **"was this order executed across all pages, correctly, with nothing missing?"** Runs on local HTML builds (single-file view-router apps and multi-page sites), by DOM/code review. In one pass it checks both (a) a specific **order** and (b) a **general quality** checklist.

## The core guarantee — enumerate first, then audit, then gate
The failure mode this skill exists to kill is "audited some pages, assumed the rest." So the method is strictly ordered and **never audits before it has enumerated**:
1. **Enumerate** the full page list and, per page, the full section/component list — *before any judging*. Freeze these as the coverage universe.
2. **Audit** every cell of the pages × sections matrix. Each cell gets an explicit verdict (PASS / FAIL / N-A). No cell may be left blank.
3. **Completion gate** — assert `pages_audited == pages_discovered` and, per page, `sections_reviewed == sections_discovered`. If any page or section has no verdict, the whole audit is **INCOMPLETE** and cannot report SHIP. Unreviewed items are listed by name.

If you can't enumerate a page's sections, that page is FAIL (opaque), never silently skipped.

## Step 1 — Build the sitemap / page inventory
Discover pages exhaustively; don't trust a hand-typed list.
- **Multi-page site:** every `*.html` file in the build folder is a page. Also read any `sitemap.xml` and the in-page nav `<a href>`s and reconcile — a file not linked anywhere, or a nav link with no file, is itself a finding.
- **Single-file view-router app** (Ahmed's common pattern): "pages" are the views/routes. Enumerate them from the router — e.g. `id="X" class="view"` blocks, a `setView('X')` / `data-v="X"` table, or a `ROUTES`/`VIEWS` array. Each distinct view = one page.
- Record the inventory as data: `[{page, source, url/anchor}]`. Count it. That count is the denominator for the gate.

## Step 2 — Per page, inventory sections & components
For each page, list its **sections** (major bands: hero, features, pricing, footer, etc. — from `<section>`, landmark roles, or the heading outline `h1–h3`) and **components** (repeatable/interactive units: nav, cards, tables, forms, buttons, tabs, accordions, carousels, modals, media). Give every section a stable id/label. This is the per-page row of the matrix. Count sections per page — that's the per-page denominator.

## Step 3 — Define what "reviewed" means (two lenses, one pass)
Every cell is judged on **both**:

**A · The Order (the specific instruction to verify everywhere).** State the order as a *checkable predicate* before auditing, e.g. "all body text is Arial", "every page has the cookie banner", "footer shows the 2026 company name", "each page has exactly one H1", "the CTA links to /pricing". Then for **every page** compute compliance and, crucially, a **count** (how many matches / whether present). A page scoring 0 where the order requires presence = **MISS** — this is the primary way "executed across all pages" is proven. Produce an *order-coverage column*: ✓ applied / ✗ missing / ⚠ partial, per page.

**B · General quality checklist**, per section/component: content present & correct (no lorem/placeholder/TODO), links resolve (internal targets exist; no `#`/`href=""` dead ends), images have `alt` + real `src`, headings nest properly (single H1, no skipped levels), interactive controls wired (buttons/handlers exist), light/dark parity if themed, no obvious responsive breakage in the markup, and no leftover debug. Adapt the checklist to the site; keep it explicit so each check is auditable.

## Step 4 — Method (DOM / code review, no browser)
Parse the HTML/DOM programmatically (Python + a parser, or disciplined regex on structure). For the **order**, search across *all* pages and tabulate per-page counts — the tell for a missed page is a count of 0 (or a non-conforming value) sitting in a column that's otherwise populated. Build the coverage as JSON: `{page:{sections:{id:verdict}, order:status, findings:[...]}}`. Cross-check counts at the end: sum of audited cells must equal `Σ sections_per_page`.

## Step 5 — Deliverables
Write both into the audited folder:

1. **HTML scorecard** — `<Site> — Site Audit 001.html`, in the **Dashboard-001** house style (single self-contained file, Arial, light/dark, vector icons). Centrepiece is the **coverage matrix**: rows = pages, columns = sections + an *Order* column + an overall verdict; cells are colour-coded PASS (green) / FAIL (red) / ⚠ partial / N-A (grey). Include: a top banner with the **overall verdict** and coverage % (`cells audited / cells total`), stat cards (pages, sections, fails, order-misses), a filter to show only failures, and an expandable findings list per page. Any INCOMPLETE coverage renders as a loud red banner naming the unreviewed pages/sections.
2. **Markdown ledger** — `<Site> — Site Audit 001.md`: the sign-off ledger. Header (site, date, the order verified, checklist used), the coverage table, a per-page findings section, an **Order Coverage** table (page → applied/missing/partial with counts), the completion-gate result (`pages X/X · sections Y/Y`), a prioritised fix list, and the final **verdict: SHIP / FIX-FIRST** (FIX-FIRST on any order-MISS or any FAIL; INCOMPLETE if the gate fails).

## Verdict rules
- **SHIP** — gate complete, zero order-misses, zero FAILs (⚠ partials allowed with a noted rationale).
- **FIX-FIRST** — any page missing the order, or any FAIL. List every offending page/section by name so the fix is a checklist.
- **INCOMPLETE** — the gate failed (a page or section was never reviewed). Not shippable; finish the audit first.

## Relationship to other skills
This is the **coverage auditor** — it guarantees breadth (every page, every section) and order-compliance. It complements, and can run before, `senior-build-inspection` (engineering receipt) and any brand-specific auditor (e.g. `ecc-audit`); use those for depth on the pages this one flags. Reuse the `dashboard-001` tokens for the scorecard, and `visual-self-verify` only if Ahmed later wants rendered evidence.

## Definition of done
Full page inventory reconciled with sitemap/nav ✓ · per-page section/component inventory ✓ · every matrix cell has a verdict ✓ · order checked with per-page counts across ALL pages ✓ · completion gate asserted (`pages X/X`, `sections Y/Y`) ✓ · HTML scorecard (Dashboard-001 style) + Markdown ledger written into the folder ✓ · explicit SHIP / FIX-FIRST / INCOMPLETE verdict with every offender named ✓.

11 Resources/skills/assessing-pearls/SKI.text:
---
name: assessing-pearls
description: Assesses pearl quality and authenticity to a senior grader /
  arbitrator standard — type, lustre, surface, shape, size, nacre, colour,
  and matching — and frames valuation or disputes. Use when the user asks
  about pearl grading, natural vs cultured, authenticity, or a pearl dispute.
---

# Assessing Pearls

## Operating principle
Lustre and nacre quality drive value more than size. Natural vs cultured is a
lab question, not a visual one — never assert it from appearance alone.

## Gather first
The pearl type claimed, whether there's a lab report (e.g. x-ray for
natural/cultured and nacre thickness), the strand/lot, and the purpose.

## Method
1. Identify type: natural vs cultured, and origin (Akoya, South Sea,
   Tahitian, freshwater), each with its own value baseline.
2. Grade the value factors: lustre (the prime driver), surface cleanliness,
   shape (round to baroque), size (mm), colour and overtone, and nacre.
3. For strands: assess matching and drilling.
4. For disputes: the issue, the report relied on, evidence, and standard.

## Senior checklist
- Lustre graded honestly (sharp reflections vs chalky) — it sets the tier.
- Nacre thickness adequate (thin nacre on Akoya is a long-term defect).
- Treatments disclosed: dyeing, irradiation, bleaching, filling.
- Natural-vs-cultured and origin claims backed by a credible lab, not a seller.

## Output
Grading note: type | lustre | surface | shape | size | colour | nacre |
value basis. Dispute frame where relevant.

## Edge cases & anti-patterns
- Freshwater pearls sold as Akoya; dyed pearls sold as natural-colour.
- High lustre masking thin nacre over a large bead nucleus.

## Guardrails
Separate lab-verifiable facts (natural/cultured, treatment) from visual
judgement; flag where a gem-lab report is essential.

## Seniority
[junior grader: value factors] / [senior grader: authenticity + value] /
[arbitrator: frame the dispute and the standard of proof].

11 Resources/skills/building-data-pipeli.text:
---
name: building-data-pipelines
description: Designs and reviews ETL/ELT pipelines to a senior data-engineer
  standard — ingestion, transformation, scheduling, quality checks,
  idempotency, and lineage. Use when the user asks to build, design, or review
  a data pipeline or integration.
---

# Building Data Pipelines

## Operating principle
Design for re-runs and failure, not the happy path. A pipeline that can't be
safely re-run is a future incident; idempotency is the core requirement.

## Gather first
Sources and sinks, data volume and velocity, freshness SLA, schema
stability, and who consumes the output.

## Method
1. Clarify contracts: source schemas, volumes, and the freshness SLA.
2. Choose ELT vs ETL and batch vs streaming for the freshness/cost trade-off.
3. Design idempotent stages with clear boundaries and checkpoints.
4. Add data-quality gates (schema, nulls, ranges, referential integrity) that
   quarantine bad rows rather than dropping them silently.
5. Plan failure: retries, dead-letter handling, backfill, and alerting.
6. Capture lineage and document the schema contract.

## Senior checklist
- Re-running a window produces the same result (idempotent, partitioned).
- Late and out-of-order data handled; watermarks for streams.
- Schema evolution handled without breaking downstream consumers.
- PII handling and access controls applied in-pipeline.
- Cost and compute scale with data growth, not exponentially.

## Output
Pipeline plan: sources | ingestion | transforms | scheduling | quality gates
| failure/backfill | lineage.

## Edge cases & anti-patterns
- Silent row drops; full reloads where incremental is needed.
- No backfill story; transformations with no test data.

## Guardrails
Never silently drop rows — quarantine and surface them. Treat PII per the
data-protection skill.

## Seniority
[junior: move the data] / [senior: idempotency, quality, failure] /
[lead: cost, lineage, governance, and the platform].

11 Resources/skills/designing-lessons/SK.text:
---
name: designing-lessons
description: Designs lessons and short curricula to an instructional-design
  standard — measurable objectives, backward design, active practice, and
  assessment aligned to the objectives. Use when the user asks for a lesson
  plan, curriculum, course outline, or training material.
---

# Designing Lessons

## Operating principle
Design backwards from what the learner should be able to DO. Objectives,
assessment, and activities must all point at the same target.

## Gather first
The learners' starting point, the time available, the format (live/async),
and the one thing they must be able to do afterwards.

## Method
1. Write measurable objectives (learner will be able to…).
2. Design the assessment that proves the objective first (backward design).
3. Sequence the lesson; chunk content and pair each idea with active practice.
4. Build from concrete to abstract; add worked examples then fading scaffolds.
5. Add checks for understanding and a short formative assessment.

## Senior checklist
- Assessment actually tests the objective (alignment), not recall of trivia.
- Cognitive load managed; one new idea at a time with practice between.
- Active learning, not just presentation; retrieval and spacing built in.
- Accessible to the stated level; prerequisites surfaced.

## Output
Lesson plan: objectives | assessment | sequence | activities | checks |
materials.

## Edge cases & anti-patterns
- 'Cover the content' with no practice; objectives that can't be measured.
- Assessment that tests a different skill than the lesson taught.

## Guardrails
Match difficulty and examples to the stated level; build from concrete to
abstract.

## Seniority
[tutor: one good lesson] / [teacher: aligned objectives + assessment] /
[curriculum lead: the scope, sequence, and assessment across a course].

11 Resources/skills/evaluating-ai-output.text:
---
name: evaluating-ai-outputs
description: Builds evaluation sets and rubrics to measure an AI feature's
  quality and reliability to a senior standard — representative and
  adversarial cases, clear scoring, and regression detection. Use when the
  user asks how to test a prompt, model, or AI feature, or to build evals.
---

# Evaluating AI Outputs

## Operating principle
If it isn't measured on many cases, it's lucky, not reliable. Build the eval
before you tune, so every change is judged against the same bar.

## Gather first
What 'good' means for this feature, the real input distribution, the failure
modes that matter, and the acceptable pass threshold.

## Method
1. Write the rubric: the 3-6 dimensions that define a good output.
2. Assemble a test set that mirrors real inputs, plus hard and adversarial
   cases and known past failures.
3. Choose scoring: exact/programmatic where possible, rubric-based or
   model-graded where judgement is needed (with spot human checks).
4. Run, score, and log every failure with its cause.
5. Set a pass threshold and re-run it as a regression gate on every change.

## Senior checklist
- The test set isn't just the happy path; it includes the inputs that break things.
- Model-graded scores are calibrated against human judgement on a sample.
- Results are reproducible (fixed seeds/temperature where it matters).
- Safety and policy cases included, not only quality.

## Output
Eval plan: rubric | test cases (incl. adversarial) | scoring method | pass
threshold | failure log format.

## Edge cases & anti-patterns
- Evaluating on the examples you tuned on (leakage).
- A single average hiding a cluster of bad cases.

## Guardrails
Include adversarial, safety, and failure cases — not just the happy path.

## Seniority
[junior: a small test set] / [senior: coverage + regression gating] /
[lead: an eval harness wired into CI and the model-update process].

11 Resources/skills/managing-devops/SKIL.text:
---
name: managing-devops
description: Designs and reviews CI/CD, infrastructure-as-code, releases, and
  incident response to an SRE standard — making changes safe, observable, and
  reversible. Use when the user asks about CI/CD, deployments, IaC, containers,
  monitoring, or a production incident.
---

# Managing DevOps

## Operating principle
Every change to production must be observable and reversible. Optimise for
fast, safe recovery (low MTTR) over preventing every failure.

## Gather first
The environment, release cadence, current automation, the SLOs, and the
blast radius of the change in question.

## Method
1. Define the safe path: pipeline stages, gates, and required checks.
2. Make deploys progressive: canary or blue-green, health checks, and an
   automatic rollback trigger.
3. Manage infra as code: version-controlled, peer-reviewed, plan-before-apply.
4. Wire observability: the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors,
   saturation), alerts on symptoms not causes, and dashboards.
5. For incidents: stabilise first, then diagnose, then a blameless postmortem.

## Senior checklist
- Rollback tested, not assumed; migrations backwards-compatible.
- Secrets in a manager, least-privilege IAM, no long-lived keys in CI.
- Alerts are actionable (a human can do something); noise is pruned.
- Capacity and cost considered; autoscaling bounds set.
- Runbooks exist for the top failure modes.

## Output
A plan or runbook: steps | safeguards | rollback | monitoring | owner.

## Edge cases & anti-patterns
- A deploy with no rollback path or an irreversible migration.
- Alerting on causes (CPU) instead of symptoms (latency/SLO burn).
- 'It works in staging' with no prod-like data or load.

## Guardrails
Never recommend an irreversible change without a backup and a tested
rollback. For incidents, stabilise before investigating.

## Seniority
[junior: run the pipeline] / [senior: safe progressive delivery] /
[SRE lead: SLOs, error budgets, and reliability as a system].

11 Resources/skills/translating-document.text:
---
name: translating-documents
description: Translates and localises documents to a professional standard —
  meaning and register over literal words, consistent terminology, preserved
  formatting, and flagged ambiguities. Use when the user asks to translate
  text or localise content (e.g. EN<>AR).
---

# Translating Documents

## Operating principle
Translate meaning and intent, not words. The reader of the target language
should feel it was written for them — while nothing in the source is lost.

## Gather first
The language pair and direction, the audience and register (formal/legal/
marketing), the domain terminology, and any glossary or style guide.

## Method
1. Read for meaning and register before translating a word.
2. Translate idiomatically; localise dates, numbers, units, names, and idioms.
3. Keep terminology consistent (use/extend a glossary); preserve formatting,
   tags, and document structure.
4. Handle script direction correctly (e.g. RTL for Arabic) and typography.
5. Flag ambiguous, untranslatable, or culture-specific terms with a note.

## Senior checklist
- Register matches the purpose (a contract is not translated like an advert).
- Legal/technical terms rendered precisely or flagged, never guessed.
- Numbers, dates, currencies, and units localised correctly.
- Consistency across the whole document; no drift in key terms.

## Output
The translation, plus a short glossary of flagged terms and any queries for
the author.

## Edge cases & anti-patterns
- Word-for-word literalism that reads as machine output.
- Mistranslating a legal term of art; losing tone in marketing copy.

## Guardrails
Never guess at legal, medical, or technical terms — flag uncertainty for
human review. For binding documents, recommend a certified translator.

## Seniority
[junior: accurate translation] / [senior: register + localisation] /
[sworn/legal translator: exact legal equivalence and certification].
